phenolphthalein_1pct.note: Simplified schematic - matches molecules/phenolphthalein.svg's caveat. Not a bond-precise organic structure; see the properties card note.

zn_metal.note: A single atom, not a molecule - a solid metal is a lattice of many of these. See molecules/zn.svg's caption.

mg_metal.note: A single atom, not a molecule - a solid metal is a lattice of many of these. See molecules/mg.svg's caption.

fe_metal.note: A single atom, not a molecule - a solid metal is a lattice of many of these. See molecules/fe.svg's caption.

cu_metal.note: A single atom, not a molecule - a solid metal is a lattice of many of these. See molecules/cu.svg's caption.

ca_metal.note: A single atom, not a molecule - a solid metal is a lattice of many of these. See molecules/ca.svg's caption.

mgo_s.note: One ion pair, drawn simply. The real solid is a cubic lattice of many magnesium and oxide ions, not a molecule.

hno3_1m.note: The nitrate group is flat - nitrogen and its three oxygens all lie in one plane.

na2co3_1m.note: The carbonate group is flat - carbon and its three oxygens all lie in one plane.

caco3_s.note: One calcium ion with one carbonate ion. The real solid is a lattice of many of these, not a molecule.

cuo_s.note: One ion pair, drawn simply. The real solid is a lattice of many copper and oxide ions, not a molecule.

nh4cl_1m.note: The ammonium ion is tetrahedral - the four hydrogens point to the corners of a triangular pyramid.

co2_g.note: Carbon dioxide is linear - the two oxygens sit exactly opposite each other at 180 degrees.

nh3_g.note: Ammonia is pyramidal, not flat: the lone pair on the nitrogen pushes the three hydrogens down to about 107 degrees apart.

fecl3_0_1m.note: Drawn with the three chlorides spread evenly around the iron. In solution the ion is surrounded by water molecules as well.

baso4_s.note: One ion pair, drawn simply. The real solid is a lattice of many barium and sulfate ions, not a molecule.

agi_s.note: One ion pair, drawn simply. The real solid is a lattice of many silver and iodide ions, not a molecule.

agbr_s.note: One ion pair, drawn simply. The real solid is a lattice of many silver and bromide ions, not a molecule.

feoh3_s.note: Three hydroxide ions spread evenly around the iron, which carries a 3+ charge here rather than the 2+ of iron(II) hydroxide.

pbcl2_s.note: One lead ion with two chlorides, drawn simply. The real solid is a lattice of many such ions, not a molecule.

rust_s.note: An Fe2O3 unit with one water molecule shown loosely attached. Rust genuinely has no fixed formula - the amount of water varies from place to place in the same flake, which is why it is written Fe2O3 with a dot and xH2O.

nacl_s.note: One ion pair. The real solid is a cubic lattice of many sodium and chloride ions - and because those ions are locked in place, the solid does not conduct.

na_metal.note: A single atom, not a molecule - a solid metal is a lattice of many of these. See molecules/na.svg's caption.

s_powder.note: A single atom, drawn simply. Solid sulfur is really made of rings of eight atoms, not single ones.

c_s.note: A single atom. In charcoal and coal, many carbon atoms are joined into sheets and networks rather than separate molecules.

n2_g.note: The two atoms are held by a triple bond - the strongest part of the reason nitrogen is so unreactive.

so2_g.note: Bent, not linear - the lone pair on the sulfur pushes the two oxygens down to about 119 degrees apart.

no2_g.note: Bent like sulfur dioxide, and the only common coloured gas in this lab.

h2co3_aq.note: The carbon and its three oxygens all lie in one flat plane.

hno3_aq.note: The nitrate group is flat - nitrogen and its three oxygens all lie in one plane.

cahco3_aq.note: A calcium ion with two hydrogencarbonate ions. Only one oxygen of each group is drawn attached to the calcium, to keep the picture readable.

h2o2_aq.note: The molecule is not flat - the two hydrogens sit on either side of the O-O bond like a half-open book.

mno2_s.note: One manganese ion with two oxide ions. The real solid is a lattice of many of these, not a molecule.

v2o5_s.note: Drawn simply as two vanadium atoms sharing five oxygens. The real solid is a layered network, not a molecule.

pt_s.note: A single atom, not a molecule - the catalyst gauze is a lattice of many of these. See molecules/pt.svg's caption.

so3_g.note: Flat and perfectly even - sulfur in the middle with its three oxygens 120 degrees apart, all in one plane.

kclo3_s.note: The chlorate ion is a pyramid - the chlorine sits above the triangle of its three oxygens, not in the middle of it.

kcl_s.note: One ion pair. The real solid is a cubic lattice of many potassium and chloride ions.

nh4cl_s.note: The ammonium ion is tetrahedral - the four hydrogens point to the corners of a triangular pyramid.

na2co3_s.note: The carbonate group is flat. The real solid is a lattice of many sodium and carbonate ions.

nh4no3_s.note: An ammonium ion beside a nitrate ion. The real solid is a lattice of many of these.

kno3_s.note: The nitrate group is flat. The real solid is a lattice of many potassium and nitrate ions.

cacl2_s.note: One calcium ion with two chlorides. The real solid is a lattice of many of these.

naoh_s.note: One ion pair. The real solid is a lattice of many sodium and hydroxide ions.

cao_s.note: One ion pair. The real solid is a lattice of many calcium and oxide ions, not a molecule.

cuso4_anhydrous_s.note: The same copper and sulfate ions as the blue crystals, but with no water in the structure at all - which is exactly why this one is white.

cuso4_5h2o_s.note: Two of the five waters are drawn, arranged round the copper ion. In the real crystal four sit around the copper and the fifth is held by the sulfate - and it is that built-in water which makes these crystals blue.

cocl2_s.note: Cobalt with two chlorides and no water at all, which is what makes this form blue.

cocl2_6h2o_s.note: Two of the six waters are drawn. In the real crystal all six surround the cobalt ion in an octahedron, and it is that shell of water which turns the blue form pink.

ag_metal.note: A single atom, not a molecule - a solid metal is a lattice of many of these. See molecules/ag.svg's caption.

pb_metal.note: A single atom, not a molecule - a solid metal is a lattice of many of these. See molecules/pb.svg's caption.

al_metal.note: A single atom, not a molecule - a solid metal is a lattice of many of these. See molecules/al.svg's caption.

cuno3_aq.note: Each nitrate group is flat - nitrogen and its three oxygens all lie in one plane.

znno3_aq.note: Each nitrate group is flat - nitrogen and its three oxygens all lie in one plane.

al2o3_s.note: Two aluminium ions with three oxide ions, drawn simply. The real solid is a rigid lattice of many of these - which is why it does not conduct until it is melted or dissolved in cryolite.

li_metal.note: A single atom, not a molecule - a solid metal is a lattice of many of these. Lithium is the least dense solid element there is.

k_metal.note: A single atom, not a molecule - a solid metal is a lattice of many of these. See molecules/k.svg's caption.

li2o_s.note: Two lithium ions to one oxide ion. Lithium is the only alkali metal that burns in air to this simple oxide.

na2o2_s.note: The two oxygens are still bonded to EACH OTHER - that surviving oxygen-oxygen bond is what makes this a peroxide rather than an oxide, and is why sodium parts company with lithium here.

mgco3_s.note: The carbonate group is flat. The real solid is a lattice of many magnesium and carbonate ions.

baco3_s.note: The same carbonate group as magnesium carbonate, with a much larger cation beside it - which is exactly why this one needs far more heat to break apart.

nabr_s.note: One ion pair. The real solid is a cubic lattice of many sodium and bromide ions.

nai_s.note: One ion pair. The iodide ion is the largest of the common halides, which is why it holds its outer electrons most loosely and reduces most readily.

nahso4_aq.note: A sulfate group that has kept ONE of its two hydrogens - which is why this salt still gives an acidic solution.

h2s_g.note: Bent like water, but at a wider angle of about 92 degrees - and unlike water it has almost no hydrogen bonding, which is why it is a gas at room temperature while water is a liquid.

agnh3_aq.note: The silver ion sits in a straight line between its two ammonia molecules. Holding it this way is what keeps a silver halide dissolved that water alone could not touch.

chloramine_g.note: Ammonia with one hydrogen swapped for a chlorine - pyramidal, like the ammonia it came from.

kscn_aq.note: The thiocyanate ion is linear - sulfur, carbon and nitrogen in a straight line.

fescn_aq.note: The iron holds the thiocyanate through its sulfur end. In solution the iron also carries water molecules that are not drawn here.

cu_nh3_aq.note: Four ammonia molecules arranged in a square around the copper ion. Each nitrogen also carries three hydrogens, drawn here for two of them only to keep the shape readable.

k2cr2o7_aq.note: Two chromium atoms joined through a single bridging oxygen - that bridge is what makes this the DIchromate rather than two separate chromates.

na2cro4_aq.note: One chromium with four oxygens in a tetrahedron. The chromium is in exactly the same +6 state as in dichromate - only the arrangement differs.

croh3_s.note: Three hydroxide ions around the chromium. This hydroxide is amphoteric - it reacts with excess alkali as well as with acid.

kmno4_aq.note: Manganese with four oxygens in a tetrahedron, in its highest oxidation state of +7.

k2mno4_s.note: The same manganese-and-four-oxygens unit as permanganate, but carrying two potassium ions instead of one - because the manganese here is +6 rather than +7.

ch4_g.note: A genuine tetrahedron - the four hydrogens point to the corners of a triangular pyramid at 109.5 degrees to each other, not to the corners of a square. Rotate it and that becomes obvious in a way the flat drawing cannot show.

ch3cl_g.note: Still tetrahedral, with a chlorine in place of one hydrogen. The chlorine is much larger, which is easiest to see by rotating the model.

c2h6_g.note: Two tetrahedral carbons joined by a SINGLE bond. That single bond can rotate freely, so the two ends spin relative to each other - something the double bond in ethene cannot do.

c2h4_g.note: FLAT. Every atom lies in one plane, and rotating the model shows it edge-on as a straight line. The double bond is what locks it that way - it cannot twist, which is why alkenes can have cis and trans forms and alkanes cannot.

c2h2_g.note: Perfectly LINEAR - all four atoms on one straight line. The triple bond allows nothing else, and rotating the model shows it stays a line from every angle.

cac2_s.note: A calcium ion beside a carbide ion, whose two carbons are triple bonded to each other. The real solid is a lattice of many of these.

c2h4br2_aq.note: The carbons are tetrahedral again, and the bond between them now rotates freely - the double bond of ethene has gone, used up in taking the two bromines on.

c2h2br4_aq.note: Four bromines, two on each carbon - a triple bond can take two lots of bromine where a double bond takes only one.

c2h5oh_aq.note: Two carbons with an OH group on the end. That oxygen-hydrogen bond is the whole reason ethanol is a liquid that mixes with water, while ethane - the same two carbons without it - is an insoluble gas.

glycol_aq.note: An OH group on EACH carbon. Two of them means twice the hydrogen bonding, which is why this is thick and high boiling where ethanol is thin and volatile.

ni_s.note: A single atom, not a molecule - the catalyst is finely divided metal, a lattice of many of these with an enormous surface area.

c6h6_l.note: PERFECTLY FLAT. Rotate it and the whole ring goes edge-on to a single straight line - every one of the twelve atoms lies in one plane. All six carbon-carbon bonds are the same length too, which is the strongest evidence that there are no separate double bonds here: the electrons are spread evenly right round the ring.

c6h12_l.note: The same six carbons, and NOT flat. This is the chair form: alternate carbons sit above and below the mean plane, because every carbon here is tetrahedral. Rotate it beside benzene and the difference between a delocalised flat ring and a saturated puckered one is unmistakable.

c6h5br_l.note: Still flat, and still a complete ring - the bromine has replaced a hydrogen rather than breaking anything open.

c6h5no2_l.note: The nitro group lies in the same plane as the ring, so the whole molecule is still flat.

c6h5so3h_aq.note: A flat water-hating ring at one end and a water-loving acid group at the other - the two halves that make a detergent work.

c2h5br_l.note: Two tetrahedral carbons with a bromine on the end. The bromine is much bigger than the hydrogens, and it is the polarity of that carbon-bromine bond that makes the carbon open to attack.

c2h5nh2_aq.note: Pyramidal at the nitrogen, exactly like ammonia - and for the same reason, the lone pair pushing the other three groups down.

naoh_ethanolic.note: Chemically the same sodium hydroxide as the aqueous bottle - it is the ethanol it is dissolved in, not the reagent itself, that changes what happens to a halogenoalkane.

phenol_s.note: The OH sits in the same plane as the ring, and the whole molecule is flat. That flatness is not decoration - it is what lets the oxygen's charge spread into the ring once the hydrogen leaves, which is why phenol is an acid and ethanol is not.

c6h5ona_aq.note: Phenol with its hydrogen gone. The charge left on the oxygen is shared into the flat ring beside it rather than sitting on one atom, which is the whole reason this ion is stable enough to form.

ch3cho_l.note: Look at the carbonyl carbon: it carries a HYDROGEN as well as the oxygen. That hydrogen is the whole difference between this and propanone, and it is what makes an aldehyde easy to oxidise. The C=O group and everything attached to it lie in one plane.

ch3coch3_l.note: Now compare with ethanal: the carbonyl carbon here has a CARBON on each side and no hydrogen at all. There is nothing to take off without breaking the chain, which is exactly why ketones fail both Tollens' and Fehling's.

ch3cooh_aq.note: The COOH group: one oxygen double bonded to the carbon, one carrying the hydrogen. It is that O-H hydrogen that comes off as an ion, not any of the three on the other carbon.

ch3coona_aq.note: With the hydrogen gone, the two oxygens become identical - the charge is shared evenly between them, and the two carbon-oxygen bonds are the same length. That sharing is why the ion is stable and the acid can form at all.

ester_l.note: The acid's O-H hydrogen has been replaced by an ethyl group from the alcohol. That single swap is the whole of esterification, and it is why the smell changes so completely.

tollens_aq.note: The silver sits in a straight line between its two ammonia molecules. This is the same diammine arrangement that keeps silver chloride dissolved - here it is holding the silver ready to be reduced back to metal.

fehlings_aq.note: Fehling's is a MIXTURE, not a molecule, so there is no true structure to draw. What is shown is a copper(II) ion with the two oxygens of a tartrate gripping it - the arrangement that stops the copper precipitating out of the alkali. Treat this as a sketch of the idea rather than as a real geometry.

cu2o_s.note: TWO coppers to one oxygen, because the copper here is +1 rather than its usual +2. The real solid is a lattice of many of these.

pcl5_s.note: Turn it and you will see the five chlorines are NOT all alike: three sit in a flat triangle round the middle and two stick straight out top and bottom. That shape is called a trigonal bipyramid, and phosphorus can only manage five bonds at all because it has empty d orbitals - nitrogen, directly above it, never forms NCl5.

ch3cocl_l.note: The carbonyl carbon and the three atoms round it lie in one flat plane, which leaves it open from above and below. Add the chlorine pulling electrons away along its bond and that carbon becomes the most exposed one in the whole family - which is exactly why this compound reacts with cold water on contact.

anhydride_l.note: Two ethanoic acid units sharing the single oxygen in the middle. Compare the two carbonyl carbons with the one in ethanoyl chloride: here they have only an oxygen pulling on them, not a chlorine, so they are less exposed and the whole molecule is correspondingly gentler.

ch3conh2_s.note: The nitrogen, the carbon and the oxygen all lie in one plane, and the nitrogen is FLAT rather than pyramidal like the one in ammonia. That flatness is the visible sign of its lone pair being pulled towards the carbonyl - which is why ethanamide is neutral instead of basic, and why the peptide links in a protein are rigid.

glycerol_l.note: Three carbons, each carrying an OH. Those three OH groups are the attachment points for the three fatty acid chains of a fat, and they are also why glycerol grips water so well that it ends up in hand cream.

fat_l.note: A real fat has three chains of seventeen carbons each - far too many to draw usefully - so the chains here are SHORTENED. What is honest in this model is the plan: one glycerol on the left with three ester links coming off it, all three pointing the same way. Turn it and you can see why fats pack together so tightly, and why straightening or kinking those chains is the whole difference between a solid fat and a liquid oil.

soap_aq.note: The chain here is SHORTENED - a real soap tail is seventeen carbons long. What matters is the shape: a charged head at one end and a long greasy tail at the other. Turn it side-on and you are looking at the reason soap works, because the head can stay in the water while the tail buries itself in the grease.

detergent_aq.note: Same shortened tail as the soap model, and the same two-ended shape - but the head is built round a SULFUR rather than a carbon. Put the two models side by side: that one swapped atom is the entire reason a detergent lathers in hard water and soap does not.

etmgbr_l.note: Follow the chain: carbon, carbon, then MAGNESIUM, then bromine. In bromoethane the bromine sat directly on the carbon and pulled electrons away from it. Slide a metal in between and the pull reverses - the metal is the one giving electrons up now, so the carbon end becomes electron-rich. Everything a Grignard does follows from that one structural change.

hcho_aq.note: Flat, and only four atoms. Count the hydrogens on the carbonyl carbon: TWO. Every other aldehyde has one there and a carbon group in the other place, and that difference is the entire reason methanal is the only carbonyl that gives a primary alcohol with a Grignard.

propan1ol_aq.note: PRIMARY. Find the carbon carrying the oxygen and count the hydrogens on it - there are two. Then open the butan-2-ol and 2-methylbutan-2-ol models and do the same count on each. One, two or no hydrogens on that carbon is the whole of what primary, secondary and tertiary mean.

butan2ol_aq.note: SECONDARY. The carbon holding the oxygen has a carbon on each side and ONE hydrogen left. That single hydrogen is what an oxidising agent takes to turn this into a ketone - and once it is gone the oxidation stops, because there is nothing else on that carbon to remove.

mb2ol_aq.note: TERTIARY, and the thing to look for is an ABSENCE. Turn the model until the carbon holding the oxygen faces you and look for a hydrogen on it - there is none, because three carbons and the oxygen have used up all four bonds. Nothing to remove means nothing for an oxidising agent to do, which is exactly the argument that explained why a ketone resists oxidation too.

propanoic_aq.note: Three carbons where the bromoethane had two. The one carrying both oxygens is the new arrival, and it came out of the air as carbon dioxide - which is worth pausing on, because building a carbon chain longer by exactly one is otherwise an awkward thing to arrange.

nabh4_aq.note: A boron with four hydrogens in a tetrahedron, and a sodium ion beside it. Open the lithium aluminium hydride model next to this one: identical shape, different central atom, and completely different behaviour. Aluminium is bigger and holds its hydrogens more loosely, which is why one reagent is fussy and the other reduces everything in reach.

lialh4_l.note: The same tetrahedral arrangement as sodium borohydride, built on aluminium instead of boron. Compare the two spheres in the middle: aluminium is noticeably larger, its bonds to the hydrogens are longer and weaker, and hydrogen leaves it far more readily. That is the whole of why this one reduces esters and acids - and why it cannot be used in water.

chi3_s.note: One carbon, three iodines and a single hydrogen, tetrahedral. The iodines are enormous next to the carbon holding them, and that crowding is why the solid is dense and why it drops out of solution the moment it forms rather than staying dissolved.

pbcl2_aq.note: The lead and its two chlorides are shown APART, with water molecules between them, because that is what dissolved means. Compare this with the copper sulfide lattice, where the ions are locked into a grid: nothing chemical distinguishes the two situations except how strongly the ions hold each other against the pull of the water. Hot water pulls harder, which is the whole trick of this separation.

cus_s.note: A block of the lattice, and the point is that there are no molecules in it - just copper and sulfide ions repeating in every direction. Turn it and look at how tightly packed it is. Small, highly charged ions gripping each other this closely is what an extremely low solubility product looks like from the inside, and it is why acid cannot prise this one apart.

zns_s.note: The same arrangement as copper sulfide, deliberately, because the difference between them is not one of pattern. Zinc holds its sulfide less tightly than copper does, so an acid strong enough to leave copper sulfide untouched pulls this apart with ease - and that single difference in grip is what puts the two metals into different analytical groups.

nh42co3_aq.note: Two ammonium ions and one carbonate. Turn the carbonate and you will find it is FLAT - three oxygens spread evenly round the carbon at 120 degrees - while each ammonium is a tetrahedron. Both shapes have turned up repeatedly in this app, and neither is an accident of drawing.

cucl4_aq.note: Turn it and count: FOUR chlorides, arranged tetrahedrally. Then look at the hexaaquacopper model with its six waters. Same copper, same +2 charge, different ligands and a different shape - and that is the entire reason one is blue and this one is yellow-green. Chloride is the bigger ligand, which is why only four will fit.

co_h2o_aq.note: SIX waters, arranged octahedrally - one at each of six directions, all at the same distance. Water here is not the solvent standing politely aside; every one of these is BONDED to the cobalt, and they have to be pushed off before anything else can take their place. Compare with the tetrachlorocobaltate model, which has four ligands and a different shape entirely.

cocl4_aq.note: Four chlorides, tetrahedral, and the same cobalt atom that sat in the middle of six waters a moment ago. Open both models side by side: nothing about the metal has changed, not its identity and not its charge, yet one solution is pale pink and this one is deep blue. That is the lesson of the whole batch - colour belongs to the complex, not to the metal.

dmg_aq.note: The molecule is flat, and the two nitrogens sit on the same side of it at a fixed distance apart. That distance is everything. It happens to match the spacing nickel wants between neighbouring bonds almost exactly, and it matches very few other ions, which is why one reagent picks nickel out of a mixture.

ni_dmg_s.note: Look at it edge-on: the whole thing is FLAT, with four nitrogens in a perfect square round the nickel. Two ligand molecules, one above the plane of the page and one below, each gripping with two nitrogens. It carries no charge at all, which is why it will not dissolve in water - and that is exactly what makes it weighable.

aloh4_aq.note: Four hydroxides round the aluminium, tetrahedral, and the whole ion carries a charge - which is the reason it dissolves where the neutral hydroxide would not. Put this beside the zincate model and they are the same shape doing the same job, which is exactly why sodium hydroxide alone cannot tell aluminium from zinc.

znoh4_aq.note: Compare this with the aluminate model and you will find nothing useful to tell them apart: same shape, same four hydroxides, both colourless in the beaker. That is the honest state of the investigation after this test - it proves zinc hydroxide is amphoteric and leaves the identification exactly where it was.

zn_nh3_aq.note: Four ammonias round the zinc. Aluminium forms nothing like this at all, and that is what finally separates the two white hydroxides. Worth noticing what is NOT here: any colour. Copper's version of this complex is deep blue, but zinc's d shell is completely full, so there is no electron jump available to absorb light - the usual reason for saying zinc is not really a transition metal.

na2cr2o7_aq.note: Two chromium atoms, each sitting in its own tetrahedron of oxygens, joined through the single oxygen they share in the middle. Turn it and find that bridging oxygen - it is the whole difference from chromate. Count the bonds on each chromium and you will find four in both ions, because the chromium is +6 either way. Nothing has been oxidised or reduced.

na2s2o3_aq.note: A sulfate tetrahedron with one corner swapped: three oxygens and one SULFUR. Find the sulfur on the outside - it is bigger than the oxygens and a different colour, and it is the atom that does all the work. Big, soft, easily distorted atoms bind big, soft metal ions like silver; small hard ones like oxygen prefer small hard ions like calcium. That one idea explains why hypo dissolves silver bromide and limewater does not.

ag_s2o3_aq.note: One silver in the middle, held by two thiosulfates, and the bonds run to their SULFUR atoms rather than to any oxygen. Trace the two bonds from the silver and check which atoms they land on - that is the hard-and-soft principle made visible, and it is the reason this complex is stable enough to strip silver bromide off a photographic film.

urea_s.note: Turn it and the whole molecule is FLAT - both nitrogens, the carbon and the oxygen lie in one plane. That is the same flatness seen in ethanamide, and for the same reason: each nitrogen's lone pair is pulled towards the carbonyl. Urea simply has two of them instead of one, which is where its unbeatable 46 % nitrogen comes from.

nh42so4_aq.note: Two ammonium ions and one sulfate. Both ions are neat tetrahedra - turn the model and each looks the same from four directions - but they behave quite differently in water: the sulfate sits there unchanged while the ammonium slowly gives a hydrogen ion back, which is what makes the solution acidic.

sio2_s.note: This is a FRAGMENT, and the fragment is the lesson. There is no silica molecule to show - every silicon here has four oxygens round it and every oxygen bridges two silicons, and the pattern simply carries on past the edges of the model in all directions. To melt sand you have to break that network apart, which is why it takes 1700 degrees, while carbon dioxide with its similar-looking formula is a gas at room temperature.

clinker_s.note: One silicate tetrahedron with three calcium ions round it. The real clinker is a lattice of these repeated endlessly - what is shown is the repeating unit, the same way a single NaCl pair stands for a whole salt crystal. The calcium is what makes wet cement so alkaline, and so good at burning skin.

cement_set_s.note: There is no molecule of set cement, so this is a SKETCH of what hardening does: silicate units, shown as grey blocks, that have grown out and locked into each other through the space the mixing water filled. The number of water molecules taken up varies from place to place in the same lump, which is why set cement has no single formula. Nothing here dried out - the water became part of the solid.

alum_aq.note: One aluminium ion between two sulfates. Notice how SMALL the aluminium sphere is for something carrying three positive charges - that combination of small size and high charge is the whole story. It pulls so hard on the water molecules around it that they let go of a hydrogen ion, which is why a solution of this salt turns litmus red, and it is the first step towards the hydroxide floc.

aloh3_s.note: Turn this one and look at the SPACE in it. Aluminium hydroxide units bridged loosely through hydroxide groups, with wide gaps everywhere - that openness is the entire reason it works. A dense precipitate would drop straight to the bottom and leave the water as dirty as before, while this mesh forms through the whole depth and carries the clay and bacteria down inside itself.

glucose_aq.note: The hydrogens are left off so the ring can be seen. Turn it and the ring is not flat - it buckles into the shape called a chair, and every OH group sticks out sideways rather than up or down. That is what makes this particular arrangement the most comfortable of all the sugars, and it is why glucose, out of all of them, is the one life runs on.

sucrose_aq.note: Two sugar rings joined through the single oxygen in the middle. Find that oxygen and follow it to the carbon on each side: those two carbons are exactly the ones that would otherwise open into reducing groups, and both are used up making this one bond. That is the whole reason sucrose gives nothing with Fehling's. The hydrogens are left off, and the fructose ring on the right is drawn as a six-membered ring for clarity when the real one has five.

invert_sugar_aq.note: The same two rings as sucrose, but no longer joined - this is a MIXTURE of two separate sugars, not one molecule, and the gap between them in this model is real rather than decorative. Compare it with the sucrose model: one bond is missing, and that is the entire difference between a negative Fehling's test and a positive one.

gluconate_aq.note: The ring has opened out into a straight chain and the end carbon now carries TWO oxygens instead of one. That is the only change Fehling's made - the aldehyde has become a carboxylate - and everything else along the chain is the glucose it came from, untouched. Hydrogens are left off.

starch_aq.note: A real starch molecule has HUNDREDS of glucose units and could not be drawn. Five are shown, each as one grey block, with the linking oxygens between them in red. What is honest here is the plan and the curve: the chain does not run straight but twists, and that twist is what eventually coils it into the helix the iodine test depends on.

starch_iodine_aq.note: Turn this one and look down the length of it: the grey sugar units spiral round, and the purple iodines sit in a straight line down the hollow middle. They touch nothing - there are no bonds drawn to them because there are none. The colour comes from iodine being TRAPPED inside the coil, which is exactly why warming the tube, which shakes the coil loose, makes the blue-black vanish.

albumin_aq.note: A real protein has thousands of atoms, so each amino acid is shown here as one grey block with the peptide nitrogens between them in blue. The point of the model is the FOLD: the chain does not lie straight, it doubles back on itself into a particular shape, and everything the protein does depends on that shape being kept.

albumin_coag_s.note: Put this beside the albumin model and count the bonds: there are exactly as many, and not one has been broken. All that has changed is where the blocks sit - the neat fold has been shaken out into a sprawl. That is denaturation, and it is why cooking an egg cannot be undone by cooling it and why a biuret test on the result still works.

biuret_aq.note: Biuret reagent is a MIXTURE - copper(II) sulfate stirred into plenty of sodium hydroxide - so there is no real structure to show. What is drawn is a copper(II) ion with hydroxide ions round it, which is the state the copper is actually in while it waits for a protein. Read it as a sketch of the bottle's contents, not as a formula.

protein_cu_aq.note: One copper ion held by FOUR peptide nitrogens at once, two from each of two stretches of chain. Count them, because the number matters: a single amino acid has no peptide link at all and gives no colour, and you need at least three joined together before there are enough nitrogens to grip the copper. That is why the biuret test detects a protein rather than an amino acid.

scum_s.note: One calcium holding TWO shortened soap chains, one above and one below. Sodium could only ever hold one; calcium's second charge lets it bridge two, and the bridged pair has no charged end left free to keep it in solution. That is scum, and it is why it will not wash off.

h3po4_aq.note: Phosphorus at the centre of a tetrahedron of four oxygens, three of which carry a hydrogen - which is what makes the acid tribasic.

toluene_l.note: Turn it edge-on and the ring is completely FLAT - that flatness is what lets the six electrons spread evenly round it, and that spreading is why benzene resists everything an alkene falls to. The methyl group is the only thing sticking out, and it pushes electron density into the ring. Compare it with the nitrobenzene model, where the group pulls the other way.

acetophenone_l.note: The carbonyl group lies in the SAME plane as the ring rather than sticking out of it, which is the visible sign that the two are sharing electrons. What the carbonyl does with them is pull - away from the ring - so this product is less reactive than the benzene it was made from, and that is the whole reason acylation stops after one substitution.

nitrotoluene_l.note: This shows the ORTHO isomer, with the nitro group next to the methyl; the para isomer, with the two opposite each other, is the other half of what the flask actually contains. The position in between is the one that gets essentially nothing, and following where the methyl pushed its electrons is what predicts that.

dinitrobenzene_s.note: Count round from one nitro group to the other: they are 1 and 3, with an empty carbon between them. That is META, and it is the opposite of the pattern the methyl group produced. Both nitro groups lie flat in the plane of the ring, sharing electrons with it - and pulling them away.

tribromophenol_s.note: Three bromines, at 2, 4 and 6 - both positions next to the OH and the one opposite it, with the two meta positions left untouched. No catalyst was needed for any of it. Set this beside the benzene model, which will not react with bromine water at all, and the size of what one OH group does to a ring is visible in a single picture.

picric_s.note: Three nitro groups all pulling electron density out of the ring, and the OH sitting among them. That pull is why the O-H hydrogen leaves so readily that this behaves as a strong acid rather than as a phenol - the same functional group, in different company, changed what class of compound it acts like.

benzoic_s.note: The ring is exactly as it was in the methylbenzene model - not one bond in it has changed. Only the group hanging off it is different, cut back by hot permanganate to a single COOH. However long the side chain was, oxidation stops here.

aniline_l.note: The nitrogen sits in the plane of the ring, not sticking out of it, and that is the whole story: its lone pair is being shared into the ring rather than pointing away from it. Two consequences from one arrangement - the ring becomes extremely reactive, and the nitrogen becomes a much weaker base than ammonia, because the pair it would use to accept a hydrogen ion is busy elsewhere.

tribromoaniline_s.note: The same 2, 4, 6 pattern the phenol gave, for the same reason and with the same lack of any catalyst. Open the two models side by side: swap the oxygen for a nitrogen and nothing else about the outcome changes.

alcl3_s.note: Flat and three-coordinate, which is unusual and is exactly the point. Most things arrange four pairs of electrons round themselves; aluminium here has only three, so there is a gap where a fourth pair could go. That gap is what makes it grab a chloride off a passing molecule and leave behind the electrophile a Friedel-Crafts reaction needs.

sn_metal.note: A fragment of the metal lattice. There are no molecules in a metal - just atoms packed together sharing their outer electrons, which is why metals conduct. Here those loose electrons are what get handed to the nitro group.

sncl4_aq.note: Tetrahedral, and the tin is now +4 - it has handed over the four electrons that reduced the nitro group to an amine. Following the reducing agent to see what it turned into is how you check a redox equation balances.

vo2_aq.note: Find the two oxygens bonded SHORT and tight to the vanadium - those are held oxide ions, not water. A +5 ion is small and charged enough to keep them permanently. Open the vanadium(III) model afterwards and they are gone; the series is a change in structure, not only in colour.

vo_aq.note: ONE oxide left, sitting straight above the vanadium, with waters filling the rest. Count them against the vanadium(V) model, which had two, and the vanadium(III) model, which has none. The oxide ions leave one at a time as the charge falls.

v3_aq.note: No oxide at all now - six waters and nothing else, all at the same distance. This is what a plain hydrated ion looks like, and reaching it is the point at which the vanadium stopped being able to hold an oxide.

v2_aq.note: The same six-water arrangement as vanadium(III), one electron richer. Nothing about the picture says how unstable it is - which is worth knowing, because a structure drawing tells you what something IS and never how long it will last.

cr2_aq.note: Six waters round a chromium(II). Put it beside the vanadium(II) model and they are the same shape doing the same thing: both sit at the bottom of their own series, and both hand their electrons to the first oxygen that comes past.

na2s4o6_aq.note: FOUR sulfurs in a row. The two in the middle were the outer sulfur of one thiosulfate and the outer sulfur of another - iodine took an electron from each and the two ends joined. Trace that chain and the two-to-one ratio the titration depends on is visible rather than memorised.

na2o_s.note: A fragment of the lattice - there are no Na2O molecules, only ions repeating in every direction. Compare it with the phosphorus(V) oxide model, which IS a molecule with a definite edge. That difference in structure is the whole reason one oxide is basic and the other acidic, and it is what Period 3 is really about.

p4o10_s.note: A cage of four phosphorus atoms with oxygens bridging between them and one more on each corner - and crucially it STOPS. This is a molecule with an edge, not a lattice that carries on, which is why it melts low, dissolves rather than merely reacting at a surface, and behaves as an acidic oxide.

sicl4_l.note: Tetrahedral, and outwardly the twin of tetrachloromethane - yet one fumes in damp air and the other is so unreactive it was used in fire extinguishers. The difference is not in this picture: silicon is the larger atom and has empty d orbitals a water molecule can bond to before any Si-Cl bond has to break. Carbon has no such opening.

na2sio3_aq.note: A single silicate unit with its sodium ions - which is exactly what silica is NOT. Open the silica model beside it and the contrast is the point: there, every silicon was locked into an endless network, and getting to this one free unit is what boiling alkali had to achieve.

alcl3_aq.note: Six waters round an aluminium ion, with the chlorides drifting free further out. Look at how SMALL the aluminium sphere is for something carrying three charges - the water molecules are held so tightly that one of them gives up a hydrogen ion, and that is the entire reason a solution of this salt turns litmus red.

diazonium_aq.note: Follow the chain out from the ring: carbon, then nitrogen, then nitrogen - and the two nitrogens are held by a TRIPLE bond, drawn short and tight. They are already most of the way to being N2, one of the most stable molecules there is, and that is the whole reason this group will leave in favour of almost anything. It is also why the compound decomposes above 5 °C.

azo_dye_s.note: Turn it edge-on: the two rings and the N=N bridge all lie in ONE flat plane. That flatness is not decoration - it is what lets the electrons run continuously from one end of the molecule to the other, and a system that long absorbs visible light instead of ultraviolet. Flat and long means coloured.

azo_dye_red_s.note: Open this beside the orange dye and look for the difference: one atom, at the far right, a nitrogen where the other had an oxygen. Everything else is identical - same two rings, same flat plane, same N=N bridge. One atom moved the colour from orange to red, which is how a dye chemist works.

c6h5i_l.note: An iodine on a benzene ring. The iodine sphere is huge beside the carbons - and that size is part of why it cannot be put here directly: iodine is too unreactive for the halogen carrier route, so this compound has to be reached the long way round through a diazonium salt.

nano2_aq.note: The nitrite ion is BENT rather than straight, because the nitrogen keeps a lone pair that pushes the two oxygens together. Compare it with the nitrate ion, which is flat and symmetrical with three oxygens - one oxygen fewer and the whole shape changes.

hno2_aq.note: Bent like the nitrite it came from, with a hydrogen on one oxygen. It is drawn here because the reaction needs it, not because a bottle of it exists - this molecule falls apart on standing, which is why it is always made in the flask and used within minutes.

cotton_cloth.note: Three cellulose chains lying alongside each other, each unit shown as one grey block. What matters is the SPACE between them. Nothing here will bond to a direct dye; the gaps are simply wide enough for a flat molecule to slip into and stay.

dyed_cloth.note: The same three chains with dye molecules sitting in the gaps between them - and notice there are NO bonds drawn from a dye to a chain, because there are none. The dye is held by nothing more than the weak attraction between surfaces in contact. That is the whole reason a direct dye eventually washes out.

polythene_s.note: SIX carbons are drawn; a real chain has tens of thousands, so this is a fragment and the ends are not real ends. Turn it and look along the backbone: there is nothing on it but hydrogens. No double bond, no oxygen, no nitrogen - nowhere for water, acid, alkali or a bacterium to get a grip. That absence is why a carrier bag outlives the person who threw it away.

pvc_s.note: The same backbone as poly(ethene) with a chlorine on every other carbon - count along and you will see the pattern. Those chlorines are bulky and they pull on the electrons around them, so the chains no longer slide over each other freely, and the material is rigid where poly(ethene) is soft. A fragment, not a whole chain.

ptfe_s.note: Turn this one end-on and look down the chain: the fluorines form a complete sheath round the carbon backbone. Nothing can reach the carbons inside, which is what makes PTFE inert to acids, alkalis and solvents alike, and what makes a pan non-stick. A fragment, not a whole chain.

polystyrene_s.note: One repeat unit shown with its benzene ring, and the ring is the point: it is enormous next to the backbone, and on a real chain there is one of these every other carbon. They physically obstruct the chains from packing tightly against each other, which is why polystyrene is hard and glassy rather than waxy.

ch2chcl_g.note: Flat, and the two carbons are held by a DOUBLE bond - drawn shorter than a single bond would be. That double bond is the whole reason this molecule can polymerise; compare it with the ethane model, where the same two carbons are joined by one bond and nothing can open.

c2f4_g.note: Flat like ethene, with four fluorines instead of four hydrogens. The fluorines are small but pull electrons hard, and the C-F bonds they make are the strongest carbon forms with anything - which is what the finished PTFE inherits.

styrene_l.note: The ring and the C=C lie in the SAME flat plane, sharing their electrons - which is why the double bond here polymerises more readily than plain ethene. Find the two carbons sticking out at the top: those are the pair that will open and join to the next molecule.

terephthalic_s.note: Look at both ends: a COOH group at the top and another at the bottom, exactly opposite. TWO reactive groups on one molecule is the entire requirement for condensation polymerisation - with only one it would join to a partner and stop, and no chain could ever grow.

polyester_s.note: One repeat unit: a benzene ring with an ester group at each end and the short two-carbon bridge that joins on to the next unit. Find the oxygens - each of those C-O-C joins is an ester link, and an ester link is a bond hot alkali can break. That is the whole reason this polymer can be recycled chemically and poly(ethene) cannot.

diaminohexane_aq.note: Six carbons in a zig-zag with a nitrogen at each end. Both ends are the SAME kind of group, which is what lets it join to something at both ends and keep a chain growing. Count the carbons - the exact number matters, because it decides how neatly the finished nylon chains lie against each other.

adipoyl_cl_l.note: A chlorine and a double-bonded oxygen at each end of a six carbon chain. Compare the ends with the diamine model: one has nitrogens, this has acid chlorides, and it is those two kinds of end meeting that makes the amide link. Using the chloride rather than the acid is what makes it happen at room temperature.

nylon_s.note: One repeat unit. Find the two places where a nitrogen sits next to a carbon carrying a double-bonded oxygen - those are the amide links, and they are the same bond that joins amino acids in a protein. In the real solid the N-H on one chain hydrogen bonds to the C=O on its neighbour, pulling the chains tightly together; that is why nylon can be drawn into a strong fibre.

glycine_aq.note: The smallest amino acid, and both kinds of group are on it at once: a nitrogen at one end, a COOH at the other. That is why glycine alone can polymerise where a polyester needs two different monomers - every molecule can join to the next at either end.

polypeptide_aq.note: Three glycine units joined. Look at the links: a nitrogen beside a carbon carrying a double-bonded oxygen, exactly what the nylon model shows. Same bond, same reaction, one made in a flask and the other made in every cell in your body. The difference in a real protein is that the side group changes from unit to unit.

na_terephthalate_aq.note: The dicarboxylic acid with its two hydrogens gone and a sodium beside each end. Put it next to the terephthalic acid model: the ring and both COO groups are identical, only the hydrogens have been swapped for sodium. Acidify it and the acid comes straight back, ready to be polymerised again.

ziegler_natta_s.note: A SKETCH, not a real geometry - a Ziegler-Natta catalyst is a mixture and the active site is a surface, not a molecule. What is worth taking from it is the titanium sitting at the centre with a vacant position on it: that gap is where each monomer docks, and because it docks in a fixed orientation every time, the side groups end up arranged regularly along the finished chain instead of at random.

isoprene_l.note: Count the double bonds - there are TWO, drawn shorter than the single bonds between them, and that is what makes this a diene rather than an ordinary alkene. The whole molecule is flat. Polymerising consumes one of these; the other is what ends up in every repeat unit of rubber, and every other entry in this batch is about what happens to it.

rubber_s.note: Two chains, and the thing to notice is what is NOT here: nothing joins them. They lie alongside each other and can slide freely, which is why raw rubber stretches and then stays stretched rather than springing back - and why solvent can float them apart one at a time. A fragment; a real chain is thousands of units long.

vulcanised_rubber_s.note: The same two chains with a SULFUR BRIDGE between them - find the two yellow atoms in the middle. That one link is the entire difference from the raw rubber model, and it changes the material completely: the chains can still uncoil when pulled but can no longer slide apart and stay put. In real vulcanised rubber there is roughly one of these per few hundred units, which is enough.

rubber_solution_aq.note: One rubber chain with solvent molecules, shown as grey blocks, in among it. This is what dissolving looks like from the inside: the solvent has got between the chains and is carrying this one off on its own. Open the vulcanised model beside it and the sulfur bridge is the reason the same thing cannot happen there.

dibromo_rubber_s.note: A chain fragment with bromines added on. They sit in pairs on adjacent carbons, which is the signature of bromine adding ACROSS a double bond rather than substituting into the chain. Their presence is the proof the double bonds were there to begin with.

o3_g.note: Three oxygens, and BENT at about 117 degrees rather than in a straight line - the middle atom keeps a lone pair that pushes the other two down. That bent, uneven arrangement is why ozone is so much more reactive than the O2 it forms from, and why it tears into a carbon-to-carbon double bond on contact.

perished_rubber_s.note: The same chain as the rubber model, except it is in PIECES - three short fragments where there was one long one. Count the carbons in any one piece and compare with the rubber model. Nothing has been added and nothing taken away; the chain has simply been cut, and a short chain cannot coil and uncoil, so the material snaps rather than stretching.

latex_aq.note: A SKETCH, not a molecule - latex is a dispersion, so what is drawn is several rubber particles as grey blocks with nothing linking them. What keeps them apart is charge, which no model of this kind can show; the point is only that they are separate objects floating in water, and that making them touch is the whole of harvesting rubber.

bakelite_s.note: Phenol rings, shown as blocks, joined by methanal bridges in THREE directions rather than two. Turn it and there is no chain to follow - every ring leads on to several others, so the whole solid is a single molecule. That is why it cannot melt or dissolve, and it is the same conclusion the vulcanised rubber model reaches by completely different chemistry.

me2sicl2_l.note: Tetrahedral, like every silicon in this batch. COUNT THE GREEN CHLORINES - there are two. That number is the only thing separating this from the two models beside it, and it decides whether what it builds is a dead end, a chain or a network.

me3sicl_l.note: Count again: ONE chlorine. Everything else about this molecule is the same shape and the same kind of bonding as the one with two, and yet it cannot build a chain at all - it can only cap one. Number of reactive ends, not their nature.

mesicl3_l.note: THREE chlorines. A chain needs exactly two ends, so three is not "better at chaining" - it is a different thing entirely, and what grows from it branches in three directions and closes into a network.

me2sioh2_aq.note: Two OH groups, pointing away from each other. One end to come from and one to go to, which is exactly what a growing chain requires.

me3sioh_l.note: One OH, and three methyls that can do nothing. Put it beside the diol: same silicon, same tetrahedron, one fewer OH, and the difference between building a polymer and stopping one.

mesioh3_aq.note: Three OH groups. Turn it and see them pointing three different ways - that is the geometric reason three ends give a network rather than a longer chain. They simply do not lie in a line.

silicone_s.note: Follow the backbone and read the atoms off in order: silicon, oxygen, silicon, oxygen. There is no carbon in it at all - the carbons are the methyl groups hanging off the sides. Two things follow, and both are why silicone exists. Si-O is much stronger than C-C, so heat that chars polythene leaves this alone; and those methyls face outward all the way along, so what water meets is a greasy surface. A fragment, not a whole chain.

silicone_resin_s.note: Every silicon here reaches onward in THREE directions through bridging oxygens, so there is no chain to follow and no separate molecule anywhere in it. Open the plain silicone model beside it: same Si-O bonding, same methyls, and the only difference is how many ways each silicon connects. That difference is the whole of thermoplastic versus thermoset.

glass_s.note: A silica network with sodium and calcium ions sitting in among it. Look for where the network STOPS - the metal ions have broken some of the Si-O-Si links, leaving loose ends instead of a continuous framework. Those breaks are why glass works at 1500 degrees rather than 1700, and why it softens gradually instead of melting at one sharp temperature. It is also why the atoms never settled into a regular lattice on cooling.

clay_dry_s.note: Two sheets shown as rows of grey blocks, stacked directly on one another. What holds a stack like this together is only weak attraction between the sheets - there are no strong bonds running from one to the next, and that is exactly why something can get in between them. The OH groups the formula names live INSIDE each sheet, which is why they take 500 degrees to remove rather than a warm afternoon.

clay_plastic_s.note: The same two sheets, now pushed further apart with water molecules sitting between them. Compare the gap with the dry clay model - that is the whole of what makes clay workable. The water is lubricating, not bonding, and no bond within either sheet has changed, which is why letting it dry puts everything back as it was.

metakaolin_s.note: The stack has gone. Turn it and there is no longer a top sheet and a bottom sheet - just blocks in no particular arrangement, which is what "disordered" means and what losing the OH groups did to the structure. Nothing here can take water back in, and that is why firing is one-way.

mullite_s.note: Aluminium and silicon linked through oxygens into a rigid framework - the repeating piece of a mullite needle. In the fired pot thousands of these needles grow across each other and lock together, and that interlocking is the hardness. None of this existed in the clay; the kiln built it.

ca_silicate_slag_s.note: A silicate tetrahedron with calcium beside it. The point is not the geometry but the pairing: an acidic oxide and a basic one have combined, exactly as an acid and a base do in a beaker, only at furnace temperature and in the solid state.

mg_silicate_s.note: The same arrangement with TWO magnesiums instead of one calcium - magnesium is smaller and carries the same charge, so more of them pack round each silicate. Structurally unremarkable; what matters is that the lining, not the charge, is what got consumed to make it.

gypsum_s.note: A sulfate tetrahedron, a calcium, and TWO water molecules - and those waters are at definite positions rather than floating anywhere. That is what makes this a hydrate: the water is part of the crystal, which is why removing it needs 150 degrees and why the solid stays dry to the touch.

plaster_s.note: TWO sulfate units and ONE water between them - which is what "half a water each" actually means, and it is easier to see here than in the formula. Compare with the gypsum model, which carries two waters for a single unit. The gap left behind is what the water rushes back into when plaster sets, and why it sets in minutes rather than hours.

zno_s.note: A block of the lattice - zinc and oxide ions alternating, with no ZnO molecule anywhere in it. What matters for extraction is simply that the oxygen is here at all: carbon wins a metal by taking its oxygen, so an oxide is what a furnace can work with and a sulfide is not.

fe2o3_s.note: Iron and oxide ions in a lattice - the ore, and chemically the same thing as the rust on a gate. Extraction is this reaction run backwards, and the blast furnace exists to do it by the thousand tonnes.

cu2s_s.note: TWO coppers to one sulfide, and each copper is only +1 rather than its usual +2. That is the whole reason this ore is unusual: the sulfide already holds electrons the copper wants back, so blowing air through takes the sulfur away as SO2 and leaves the copper as metal - no carbon needed anywhere.

co_g.note: Two atoms, one bond - but it is a TRIPLE bond and one of the strongest in all of chemistry, which is exactly why carbon monoxide is such a good reducing agent: it is desperate to pick up one more oxygen and become carbon dioxide, and it will take that oxygen off almost any metal ore. The same tightness is why it grips haemoglobin and will not let go.

hgo_s.note: Mercury and oxide, drawn as a chain because that is roughly how the solid is built. The bond length is the thing to notice against the zinc oxide model: mercury holds oxygen loosely, and loosely enough that a flame alone is sufficient to take it apart into the two elements. No reducing agent appears in that reaction at all.

hg_l.note: Loose atoms with no bonds drawn between them, because there are none worth drawing - mercury atoms hold each other so weakly that the metal cannot manage to be a solid at room temperature. Every other metal in this app is a rigid lattice; this one rolls.

au_metal.note: A rigid lattice of gold atoms, and the interesting thing is what never happens to it. Nothing in air, water or any single acid can pull an electron off gold, so this arrangement survives indefinitely - which is why gold is dug out of the ground already metallic and why it needed no chemistry at all to be used.

pig_iron_s.note: Iron atoms in a lattice, with carbon atoms sitting in the gaps between them rather than bonded into a compound. Turn the model and look at how crowded those gaps are. A metal bends because its layers of atoms slide past one another, and there is no room here for that to happen - so pig iron snaps instead. Compare it directly with the steel model.

steel_s.note: The same lattice as pig iron with one carbon atom in it instead of three. That is the entire difference between a metal that shatters and one that can be rolled into car-body sheet, drawn into wire and welded - and it is why steelmaking is a process of taking things out rather than putting things in.

cementite_s.note: Iron carbide, and the reason the last one per cent of carbon matters so much. Particles of this hard, brittle compound sit scattered through steel and obstruct the sliding of the iron layers, which is what hardness is. More carbon means more of these particles: harder steel, and more brittle with it. The whole difference between a car panel and a chisel is how much of this there is.

ca3po42_s.note: A phosphate tetrahedron with calcium ions around it. Phosphorus oxide is acidic and quicklime is basic, so the two combine and the phosphorus leaves the metal as this slag - which is exactly why the steel furnace has to be lined with something basic rather than silica. The same compound is the mineral part of bone, which is why bone meal worked as a fertiliser long before anyone knew why.

al_oxide_layer_s.note: Aluminium metal with a single layer of oxygen sealing the top face - roughly to scale, because the real film is only a few atoms thick. The point to see is that it is UNBROKEN. Aluminium oxide crystals are close enough in size to the metal that the film covers everything; rust is bulkier than the iron it came from, so it flakes and lets the next layer be attacked. Same idea, opposite outcome.

anodised_al_s.note: The same metal under a film grown several times thicker by electrolysis - and on a real article the difference is a factor of about a thousand, more than can be drawn here. Note which electrode does it: the aluminium is the ANODE, the opposite of every plating process, which is where the name comes from. The thickened film resists scratching, and takes dye while it is still porous.

cr_metal.note: A lattice of chromium atoms. On paper this metal should corrode - it sits well above copper in the reactivity series - and in practice a chrome bumper stays bright for decades, because of a film too thin to draw at this scale. Reactivity predicts what a metal wants to do, not always what happens to it.

cr2o3_s.note: Chromium and oxide ions alternating. This is the film that makes stainless steel stainless, and its special virtue is repair: break it and the chromium exposed underneath oxidises again in seconds, so the protection returns on its own. Paint cannot do that, and neither can a tin coating - which is the whole reason chromium is worth alloying into steel.

stainless_s.note: An iron lattice with some sites taken by chromium, and oxygen sealing the surface. Find the iron atoms and note that nothing has been done to them - they are as ready to rust as they ever were. Enough chromium is present that its oxide film covers the whole surface, so water and oxygen never reach the iron at all. The protection is an arrangement at the surface, not a change in the metal underneath.
